scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Alamikkali originated as a folk commemoration of the Battle of Karbala during Muharram.
The festival was historically organized and led by Hindustani-speaking Hanafi Muslim families known as Sahibs or Tuluker, who settled around Puthiyakota and regional forts during Tippu's campaign.
Over time, the tradition evolved into a unique cross-religious observance where the role of the Alami is performed by members of the Hindu faith.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The festival is observed during Muharram to commemorate the Battle of Karbala and honor Hazrat Imam Hussain and his fallen soldiers.
The black body coating recalls the dark clothing of opposing armies, while the final ceremony involves lighting a fire and rolling in the flames to respect slain combatants.
The rite of Vellikkaram symbolizes the memory of Imam Hussain's burial.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers move in small itinerant groups of five to six members, visiting homes across villages.
They process barefoot with inflated energy, creating noise using hand-held sticks and attached bells.
Before each residence, they lay down their alms collection vessels and execute an energetic, unstructured dance in front of the house without giving strict priority to rhythmic precision.
Watch for Alami Processional Step, Flame Rolling.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is predominantly vocal and percussion-driven by the participants themselves.
Dancers carry sticks and bells which they strike and shake during their procession and dance to produce rhythmic sound.
Listen for the Sticks, Bells.
The pulse is Unstructured / freeform vocal meter.
A resonant acoustic blend of barefoot stepping, metallic bell ringing, wooden stick strikes, and group vocal chanting featuring the characteristic 'lassolayma' refrain.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers apply black charcoal all over their bodies, decorated with white spots.
They wear dhotis drawn up to the knees, caps made of spathe containing Ixora coccinea flowers, and chains of flowers and leaves around their necks.
False beards and moustaches are constructed from munda plant fibers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Rasool Sahib is documented as a notable historical fakir sahib from Echikkanam who organized and conducted the last traditional Alamikkali ceremonies.
Celebrations are centered at Alamippalli in Kasargod district, with regional observances also conducted in Chithari, Kottikulam, and parts of Mangalore in Karnataka state.

The tradition is handed down through Hanafi Muslim fakir families (such as the Echikkanam family line of Rasool Sahib) who lead the organization, while the performance roles are inherited and maintained by Hindu villagers.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Alamikkali is a sacred memorial festival commemorating the martyrs of Karbala. Outsiders should respect the holy nature of the ritual fire ceremonies, alms collection, and cross-religious sacred spaces.
